passage: Francis had rehearsed it for a week. After tuition, near the colony gate, he asked Sunaina if she'd come with him to the farewell. She looked at her shoes and said, gently, that she liked him but only as a friend. He nodded, said "cool, cool," and walked home past the vegetable carts without seeing any of them. In the flat he shut the bathroom door and ran the tap so his mother wouldn't hear. His chest felt crushed, as if the whole building sat on it. At dinner he pushed dal around his plate. His mother didn't ask questions. She just left a cup of cocoa outside his door. Around midnight he texted his cousin, "Can I call?" They talked until two.

qa.q: Where did Francis ask Sunaina to go with him to the farewell?
qa.a: He asked her near the colony gate after tuition.

qa.q: What shows that Francis felt overwhelmed by the rejection?
qa.a: He walked home without noticing anything, cried behind a running tap, felt his chest crushed and could not eat his dinner.

qa.q: How did his mother support him, and why did it help?
qa.a: She did not push him to talk; leaving cocoa by his door showed care while giving him the privacy he clearly wanted.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Sunaina to say no?
qa.a: It was probably uncomfortable for her too; looking at her shoes and speaking gently suggest she cared about not hurting him.

grounding: Shows a teen processing the acute, crushing pain of a romantic rejection in a city home.

passage:
"Sharmila, you haven't come out all day."
"Leave it, Irfan bhaiya."
"Is it the girls from class?"
"They made a new group chat. Without me. I saw the screenshot at lunch. They were planning Saturday."
"Maybe it's a mistake—"
"It's not a mistake! Six years, bhaiya. Six years, and they just... cut me out." Her voice cracked. "I keep thinking I did something. I keep scrolling back to check."
"Okay. Stop scrolling for now. Give me the phone."
"Why?"
"Because you'll read it forty times and feel worse each time. I'll keep it on the table. You can have it back whenever."
A long pause. "It hurts right here." She pressed her ribs.
"I know. Come, walk with me to the milk booth. You don't have to talk."

qa.q: What did Sharmila see at lunch?
qa.a: She saw a screenshot of a new group chat made without her.

qa.q: What is Sharmila worried about as she keeps scrolling back?
qa.a: She fears she did something wrong to be dropped after six years, and she is searching for a reason to make sense of the pain.

qa.q: Why was Irfan's offer to hold the phone a helpful step?
qa.a: It broke the loop of rereading and gave her a pause without taking control, since she could have it back whenever she wanted.

qa.q: What would change if Irfan had said the friends weren't worth crying over?
qa.a: Sharmila might have felt dismissed and pulled further away, because her hurt about six years of friendship would not have been heard. 🫂

grounding: Shows a teen in acute pain after being socially shut out, with a sibling helping her through it.

passage: Shankar ended it by text on a Tuesday night, two lines, polite. I read it standing in the kitchen and forgot I was holding a glass of water until it tipped. For about a week, I was not a person. I deleted all our photos, then panicked and restored them from the bin. I'd be fine in class and then a song in the canteen would make my eyes sting. My sister made me run with her every morning ("Up, Jasleen, shoes on"), which I hated at first. Running was the only time my head went quiet. Looking back now, a couple of months later, I don't hate him. I was just so sure I'd be with him forever. It still pinches when I pass his street, but it doesn't knock the air out of me.

qa.q: How did Shankar end the relationship?
qa.a: He ended it with a polite two-line text on a Tuesday night.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen delete the photos and then restore them?
qa.a: Jasleen was torn between wanting to erase the pain and being afraid to lose the memories, which shows how confused and raw she felt.

qa.q: What helped Jasleen, and why did it work?
qa.a: The morning runs with the sister, because moving quieted the racing thoughts and gave Jasleen a steady routine with someone who cared.

qa.q: How might Jasleen's sister have seen that first week?
qa.a: She probably saw Jasleen hurting and chose a practical way to help, persisting even when Jasleen hated the runs at first.

grounding: A teen looks back on processing the overwhelming pain of a romantic breakup and how it eased.

passage: Class teacher's note, Wednesday. Divyansh, usually first to answer, has not raised his hand since Monday. Today he sat by the window with his hood up in the heat and left his lunch unopened. His friends told me, carefully, that he had asked Zainab to go to the school fair with him and she had said no in front of a few people. Zainab looked uncomfortable too and has been sitting at the other end of the room. At break I asked Divyansh to help me carry books to the staffroom. On the stairs he said, 'It's stupid. It feels like my chest is full of stones.' I told him it wasn't stupid. Next step: I have let his parents know he's having a hard week and mentioned the counsellor's hours to him; I'll check in on Friday. I'll also speak quietly with Zainab so she doesn't feel blamed.

qa.q: What did Divyansh leave unopened?
qa.a: His lunch.

qa.q: What does 'my chest is full of stones' reveal about Divyansh?
qa.a: It shows he is in real, heavy pain from the rejection, even though he calls it stupid.

qa.q: Why was asking him to carry books a good move?
qa.a: It gave him a private, low-pressure moment to talk without being singled out in class.

qa.q: How might Zainab be feeling this week?
qa.a: She seems uncomfortable, perhaps awkward about how the no happened, even though she was free to say no.

grounding: Shows a teenager overwhelmed by the pain of a public romantic rejection, noticed and supported by a teacher.

passage: Saturday, late. Chinmay's birthday was today. I found out from the photos. Seven of them at the new cafe near the station, all from his coaching batch, cake on his face. Last year it was just us two on my terrace with samosas. He didn't even tell me there was a plan. I keep opening the photo and closing it. My whole body feels heavy, like after a fever, and I snapped at Amma when she asked if I'd eaten. I'm not angry at her. I don't even know if I'm angry at him. Maybe I'm just not his best friend anymore and nobody told me. Tomorrow I'll go for a long cycle ride early. Maybe I'll tell Amma. Maybe. – Ramesh

qa.q: Where was Chinmay's birthday celebrated this year?
qa.a: At the new cafe near the station.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh snap at Amma?
qa.a: Ramesh was hurting from being left out and the pain spilled onto Amma, though Ramesh says it isn't anger at her.

qa.q: What would you advise Ramesh for tomorrow?
qa.a: Go on the ride and then talk to Amma or someone Ramesh trusts; later Ramesh could ask Chinmay honestly what changed.

qa.q: How might Chinmay see this if Ramesh told him?
qa.a: Chinmay may not have realised how much leaving Ramesh out hurt, and might feel sorry or awkward.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager's acute pain at being dropped by a best friend.

passage: In the small town, the bus stop was the only place to talk privately. Jyoti, seventeen, had finally told the boy from her coaching class how she felt. He'd looked at the road and said, "I don't feel that way. Sorry." The bus came. She got on and sat at the back. Her friend Sabina sat beside her and didn't say anything for three stops. Then Jyoti whispered, "It hurts everywhere." Sabina held her hand. At home, Jyoti's mother noticed her red eyes and made ginger tea without asking questions. That night Jyoti cried into her pillow, but she woke up still breathing, still herself.

qa.q: Where did Jyoti tell the boy how she felt?
qa.a: At the bus stop.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when she whispered "It hurts everywhere"?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and heartbroken by the rejection.

qa.a: She stayed close and quiet, letting Jyoti feel the pain without pressure to talk.

qa.q: How might Jyoti's mother see her red eyes?
qa.a: She understands something hurt her daughter and chooses gentle care over questions.

passage: In a flat in Copenhagen, Bilal, sixteen, read Ulla's message three times: "I think we should just be friends. I'm sorry." They'd been together four months. He put the phone face down, then picked it up again. He didn't go to football. He didn't eat dinner. His father knocked on his door at nine and sat on the edge of the bed. "Bad day?" Bilal's voice cracked. "She ended it." His father nodded slowly. "That hurts like nothing else at your age. Want to walk?" They walked to the harbour in the cold and didn't talk much. Bilal came back tired, but less alone.

qa.q: How long had Bilal and Ulla been together?
qa.a: Four months.

qa.q: What does Bilal skipping football and dinner suggest?
qa.a: He was overwhelmed and heartbroken, too hurt to carry on as normal.

qa.q: Which choice by Bilal's father helped, and why?
qa.a: Sitting with him and offering a walk, because it gave comfort without forcing him to talk.

qa.q: How might Ulla be feeling after sending the message?
qa.a: She may feel sad or guilty too, even if she believed it was the right decision.

grounding: Shows a teenager processing the acute pain of a breakup with his father's quiet support.

passage: The farewell dance list went up on the hostel noticeboard on Thursday. Simran, seventeen, had asked Varun to be her partner the week before. His name was next to Kritika's. Nobody had told her. She read it twice, then walked back to her room very carefully, as if she might break. Her roommate Dolma found her sitting on the floor with her back against the bed, not crying, just staring. "Simran?" "He said he'd think about it," Simran said. "I thought that meant yes." Then the tears came, hard. Dolma sat down beside her and put an arm around her. Later, Dolma brought her dinner from the mess and they watched a silly film on Dolma's laptop. Simran barely ate, but she stayed.

qa.q: Where did the farewell dance list go up?
qa.a: On the hostel noticeboard.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling when she walked back to her room very carefully?
qa.a: She felt shocked and deeply hurt, as if she might break.

qa.q: What did Dolma do that helped?
qa.a: She sat with Simran, held her, brought dinner and kept her company without pushing her to talk.

qa.q: How might Dolma have felt finding Simran on the floor?
qa.a: Dolma probably felt worried and sad for her friend.

grounding: A hostel student processes the pain of romantic rejection with her roommate's support.

passage:
Dear Sangeeta Akka,
I know you're busy with your exams, so sorry for the long letter. Pooja stopped being my friend. Six years, Akka. Since Class 4. She's been sitting with the new girls, and yesterday I asked her if I did something wrong, and she said, "No, we've just grown apart." Like it was nothing. I came home and couldn't eat. I keep checking her status to see if she's sad too. She isn't. Everything reminds me of her: the swing, our walk to the bus. It feels like someone died, which is stupid, because nobody died. Amma says I'll make new friends. I told her it doesn't help. Can you call me on Sunday?
Keerthana

qa.q: How many years were Keerthana and Pooja friends?
qa.a: Six years.

qa.q: How does Keerthana feel after Pooja's words?
qa.a: Keerthana feels heartbroken and overwhelmed, unable to eat and missing Pooja everywhere.

qa.q: What could help Keerthana through this?
qa.a: Talking to Sangeeta on Sunday, and being allowed to feel sad instead of being told to move on quickly.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel reading the letter?
qa.a: She would likely feel worried and protective, wanting to call and comfort Keerthana.

passage: "You asked what happened with me and Ananya, Ritu. I'm Vaibhav, and okay, here it is. She ended it by text. Two lines. 'I think we should just be friends. Sorry.' passage:
I'm Wasim, Ritu's neighbour. We share a wall, so I heard more than I should have last week.
On Monday she was on the phone on the balcony, laughing. On Tuesday the laughing stopped. That night I heard her say, "But you said," and then nothing, then crying that went on a long time.
For three days she didn't come down for badminton. Her mother bought her favourite samosas and left them outside her door. I saw the plate still full the next morning.
On Friday she came down, hair tied tight, eyes puffy, and played badminton like she was angry at the shuttle. She didn't say what happened, and I didn't ask. I just kept passing her the shuttle. At the end she said, "Thanks. Same time tomorrow?"

qa.q: Where was Ritu when she was laughing on Monday?
qa.a: On the phone on the balcony.

qa.q: What might Ritu have been feeling when she played badminton on Friday?
qa.a: She probably still felt hurt and heartbroken, maybe angry too, playing hard as if to let it out.

qa.q: What made Wasim's way of helping work?
qa.a: Wasim didn't push her to talk; he just kept passing the shuttle, which gave Ritu company without pressure.

qa.q: How might Ritu's mother have felt when the samosa plate stayed full?
qa.a: She probably felt worried and helpless, trying to comfort her daughter in a quiet way.

passage:
Week one: When Sharmila told Vishal she wanted to "just be friends," he said "cool, no problem" and walked home fast. That night he couldn't eat. His chest ached like he'd run too far. He deleted all their photos, then sat up at two looking for them in the recycle bin.
Week two: He skipped the class they shared, twice. His older brother found him lying on the floor with music loud and sat down beside him. "Rejection hurts like a real injury," his brother said. "You don't have to be okay yet." Vishal cried for the first time.
Week four: He sat in class again, two rows behind her. It still stung when she laughed. But he could say hi, and mean it a little.

qa.q: What did Vishal say when Sharmila said she wanted to be friends?
qa.a: He said "cool, no problem" and walked home fast.

qa.q: How did Vishal feel on the first night?
qa.a: He felt crushed and hurt; he couldn't eat and his chest ached like he'd run too far.

qa.q: How did Vishal's brother help, and what else could help?
qa.a: He sat beside Vishal and said he didn't have to be okay yet; talking to a trusted adult or friend and keeping small routines could also help.

qa.q: What might it be like for Sharmila to see Vishal skip their class?
qa.a: Sharmila may feel guilty and uncomfortable, caring about him but not wanting to change her answer.

grounding: Tracks a teen's acute heartbreak over several weeks after romantic rejection.

passage:
Gurleen, you think I don't understand because I'm old? Listen.
When I was a girl of sixteen, my best friend Harjot suddenly started sitting with other girls. No fight, nothing. Just gone. I, Dilnaz, felt like someone had pulled the floor away. I went to school and came home and cried in the bathroom so my mother wouldn't hear. I didn't eat my lunch for weeks.
My Nani noticed. She didn't lecture. She took me to the market every evening to help her carry vegetables, and on the walk she let me talk or not talk.
It didn't make Harjot come back. But slowly the ache got smaller than my day.
So, beta, cry if you need to. And come to the market with me this evening.

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz cry so her mother wouldn't hear?
qa.a: In the bathroom.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel when Harjot started sitting with other girls?
qa.a: She felt heartbroken and lost, as if someone had pulled the floor away.

qa.q: What choice inside the story helped Dilnaz most?
qa.a: Going to the market each evening with Nani, where she could talk or stay quiet, slowly made the ache smaller.

qa.q: How might Nani have felt watching Dilnaz stop eating lunch?
qa.a: Nani probably felt concerned and protective, which is why she found a gentle way to be near her.

grounding: An elder remembers the overwhelming pain of a friend's rejection at sixteen and what helped.

passage: The chemistry practical was at eight the next morning, and the power had gone out across the colony in the rain. Nirmala sat by the window with a candle, rereading the message from Keerthana: "I think we've grown apart. I need some space from us." Ten years of friendship, since they had shared a bench in Class 2. Her chest felt tight, as if the air had been pressed out of it. She tried to revise titration steps and read the same line six times. When her mother came in with a torch, Nirmala said, "I'm fine," then burst into tears. Her mother sat beside her and held her until the rain eased. Then they read the titration steps aloud together, one at a time.

qa.q: What time was the chemistry practical?
qa.a: At eight the next morning.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling as she reread Keerthana's message?
qa.a: She felt hurt and overwhelmed, her chest tight, as if ten years of friendship had been pulled away at once.

qa.q: What helped Nirmala get through the night before the practical?
qa.a: Letting herself cry with her mother, then reading the steps aloud one at a time, made both the grief and the revision manageable.

qa.q: What might Keerthana have been feeling when sending the message?
qa.a: Keerthana may have felt guilty or conflicted, needing space but knowing it would hurt a friend of ten years.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager's overwhelming pain at being dropped by a best friend, on a stormy night before an exam.
